title: Mowgli's Brothers
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
One night, a hungry tiger named Shere Khan came near a family of wolves. He was hunting people, but the human family escaped. Their baby crawled into the wolves’ cave. Mother Wolf called him Mowgli and protected him. Shere Khan returned and demanded the child. Mother Wolf refused. She said the baby belonged with her family now. Father Wolf agreed to raise him.

At the wolves’ meeting, Shere Khan argued that Mowgli should be given back. The young wolf leader listened. Under the Law of the Jungle, two members of the pack could speak for a cub who had no wolf parents. Baloo, a brown bear who taught the cubs, promised to teach Mowgli. Bagheera, a black panther, offered a freshly killed bull as a gift. The pack accepted the boy.

Mowgli grew up among the wolves. Baloo taught him the words and rules that helped animals live together. Bagheera showed him how to watch, listen, and move quietly. Mowgli learned quickly, but Shere Khan still hated him. The tiger waited for a chance to take him.

When Mowgli was older, Bagheera warned him that the pack’s old leader was becoming weak. Shere Khan was persuading younger wolves to forget their laws. Mowgli needed to face the danger. Bagheera told him to bring the red flower from the village, because fire frightened the animals. Mowgli went toward the human homes. He did not know whether he would stay with the wolves forever, but he knew that he had to protect the family that had raised him.

B1.text:
In the forest, a tiger named Shere Khan was hunting when a human family escaped from him. Their baby wandered into a wolf cave. Mother Wolf chose to keep the child and named him Mowgli. Shere Khan came to the entrance and demanded his prey. She stood between the tiger and the baby. Father Wolf also decided that Mowgli would grow up with their cubs.

At the pack’s meeting, Shere Khan complained that the humans’ child did not belong among wolves. The Law of the Jungle allowed two outsiders to speak for a cub. Baloo, the bear who taught young animals, offered to teach Mowgli. Bagheera, the panther, gave the pack a bull he had killed. The wolves accepted both the gift and the promise, so Mowgli became part of the pack.

As the boy grew, he learned the animals’ languages, paths, and customs. Baloo taught him the rules that kept the jungle peaceful. Bagheera showed him how to notice danger before it was close. Mowgli was clever and brave, though he sometimes forgot that he was smaller than the animals around him. Shere Khan continued to watch him and waited for the moment when the wolves would leave him unprotected.

Years later, Bagheera explained that the pack’s old leader was losing his strength. Shere Khan was using this change to turn the younger wolves against Mowgli. The panther urged the boy to find fire, which the animals feared, and to return prepared. Mowgli went toward the village to bring back the red flower. He felt pulled between two homes: the people he had not known and the wolf family that had raised him. He understood that the coming choice would change his place in the jungle.

title: Kaa’s Hunting
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Mowgli had gone looking for excitement, even though Baloo had warned him not to trust the Bandar-log, the noisy monkeys. The monkeys had no laws and often made promises they forgot. They watched Mowgli while he was alone, then carried him high into the trees. Mowgli called to them, but they only laughed and ran across the branches.

The monkeys took Mowgli to an old place among broken buildings. They wanted him to teach them how to build shelters and make plans. Mowgli knew they had taken him against his will. He tried to stay calm and sent a message through birds to Baloo and Bagheera. The two friends hurried after him, but the monkeys moved too quickly through the trees.

Baloo and Bagheera knew they needed help. They found Kaa, a very large python who could climb and move silently. Kaa listened to their story. The monkeys were afraid of him, but he agreed to help because Mowgli was in danger. Together they reached the old buildings. Baloo and Bagheera distracted the monkeys while Kaa climbed over the walls.

Kaa moved his body in a slow, powerful pattern. The monkeys could not stop watching him. They became confused and lost their courage. Kaa found Mowgli and carried him away from the ruins. Baloo and Bagheera followed. Mowgli was tired and sore, but safe. His friends reminded him that curiosity was not a reason to ignore every warning. Mowgli understood that his choices had put them all in danger, and he thanked them for coming.

B1.text:
Baloo had warned Mowgli that the Bandar-log were unreliable, but the boy was curious about them. When he wandered away, the monkeys seized him and carried him across the treetops. They wanted him to show them how to build and make plans. Mowgli knew they were not listening to him. He sent a message to his friends with a bird and waited for help.

Baloo and Bagheera hurried after the monkeys. They could not move through the branches as quickly as the Bandar-log, so they searched for someone who could. They found Kaa, an old python whose size and quiet movements made the monkeys nervous. Kaa heard that Mowgli had been taken and agreed to join the rescue. The three animals followed the trail to a ruined human settlement.

The monkeys kept Mowgli among the broken walls. They talked about making him their teacher, but they could not agree on a plan. Baloo and Bagheera drew some of them away while Kaa climbed into the ruins. The python used a slow, steady movement that held the monkeys’ attention. Their confidence disappeared. Kaa reached Mowgli and helped him escape.

Once they were beyond the ruins, Mowgli thanked the rescuers. Baloo and Bagheera were relieved, but they also explained why they had warned him about the monkeys. Mowgli had wanted to discover something new and had ignored the danger. His curiosity had become a problem for everyone who cared about him. He learned that courage does not mean refusing advice. A person can be curious and still listen carefully, especially when friends explain a real risk.

title: Tiger! Tiger!
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After Mowgli was sent away from the wolf pack, he walked to a human village. The villagers were surprised by the boy from the forest. Messua welcomed him because he looked like the son she had lost. Mowgli stayed in her home and began to learn human ways. He wore clothes, ate meals at a table, and practiced the village language. He was kind to Messua, but village life felt strange to him.

The villagers asked Mowgli to watch their cattle. While he was away, Buldeo told stories about Shere Khan, the tiger who hunted nearby. Mowgli already knew the tiger and learned that Shere Khan still planned to kill him. He spoke with his wolf brothers and made a plan. The cattle would enter a narrow valley from both ends and trap the tiger.

Shere Khan was resting in the valley after eating. Mowgli and the wolves led the herds toward him. The frightened cattle rushed forward, and the tiger could not escape. Mowgli found that the danger had ended. He took the tiger’s skin as proof that Shere Khan would not threaten him again.

When Mowgli carried the skin into the village, the people became afraid. They thought he had used magic and chased him away. Messua had cared for him, but she could not change the villagers’ minds. Mowgli returned to the forest with his wolf brothers. He had learned how humans lived, yet their fear meant he could not stay. He would have to decide later where he belonged.

B1.text:
When Mowgli left the wolf pack, he made his way to a human village. The villagers had never met a boy who had grown up among animals, so they looked at him with suspicion. Messua, however, believed that Mowgli might be her lost child. She brought him into her home and taught him ordinary human customs: wearing clothes, eating at a table, and speaking with people. Mowgli appreciated her kindness, although he still felt most at ease outdoors.

The village gave him the task of watching its cattle. Buldeo, an older storyteller, spoke often about Shere Khan, the tiger that lived nearby. He assumed Mowgli knew nothing about the forest. Mowgli learned from his wolf brothers that the tiger was still looking for him. Together they planned to use the valley’s shape to trap Shere Khan between two herds.

The tiger had eaten and was sleeping in the valley. Mowgli guided one group of cattle while his wolf brothers brought another from the opposite end. The animals rushed forward, leaving Shere Khan no clear escape. The danger to Mowgli was over. He took the tiger’s skin, hoping the villagers would understand that the threat had ended.

Instead, the villagers were frightened by Mowgli and accused him of using magic. They forced him to leave. Messua had offered him a place in her family, but she could not make the others trust him. Mowgli returned to the jungle with the wolves. His time in the village had taught him human habits, but it had also shown him how fear can separate people. For now, the forest was the only home where he could live freely.

title: The White Seal
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Kotick was a young seal born on an island where many seals gathered each year. He was different from the others because his fur was white. At first, the other seals stared at him, but his mother cared for him. Kotick grew strong and enjoyed swimming in the sea.

One day he saw hunters arrive. They drove seals across the beach and killed many for their skins. Kotick was shocked. He tried to warn the other seals, but the adults believed that the hunting would always happen. They told him that the island was their home and that he should stop worrying.

Kotick could not accept this answer. He traveled through the ocean to look for a safe place. He met many sea animals and visited faraway shores. Some beaches were beautiful, but people came there too. Kotick kept going. He learned how to swim through deep water and how to find food in different places. The journey was long, and more than once he wondered whether a safe island existed.

At last Kotick found a hidden beach protected by rocks and difficult waves. People could not easily reach it. He returned to his home island and told the other seals what he had discovered. They did not believe him immediately. Kotick challenged them to follow him and see for themselves. The seals swam behind him across the sea. When they reached the quiet beach, they understood why he had kept searching. Kotick had found a place where their young could grow without hunters.

B1.text:
Kotick was born among a large group of seals that returned each year to an island. His white coat made him unlike the other young seals, but his mother cared for him. He learned to swim, hunt for fish, and rest on the shore. He believed the island was a safe place until he saw what the hunters did.

Men arrived and drove the seals into groups. They killed many animals for their skins. Kotick was frightened by the sight and tried to tell the adults what had happened. The older seals explained that the hunters had come for years. They thought nothing could change and advised Kotick to accept the danger. He could not agree. If the same thing happened each season, the young seals would never be safe.

Kotick began a long search through the ocean. He asked sea creatures about other islands and explored distant coasts. He learned that a beach might look peaceful but still be visited by people. His journey tested his strength. He swam through rough water, searched for food, and continued even when he had not found a safe home. He became more certain that he had to keep looking, because the old island offered no protection.

Eventually Kotick reached a sheltered beach surrounded by rocks and strong waves. It was difficult for people to land there, and the seals could rest without being disturbed. Kotick returned to his community and described the place. The adults doubted him, so he invited them to follow his route. When the seals reached the hidden shore, they saw that his search had found a real answer. Kotick’s patience gave the group a chance to live more safely.

title: Down the Rabbit-Hole
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Alice was sitting outside with her sister when she saw a white rabbit hurry past. The rabbit wore a waistcoat and looked at a watch. It worried aloud that it was late. Alice had never seen an animal act this way. She followed it across a field and down a large rabbit hole. The hole went deep into the earth. Alice fell slowly past shelves and pictures, wondering where she would land.

At last she reached a room with many doors. They were all locked. On a glass table she found a tiny golden key. It opened a small door, but the doorway was too low for Alice. Through it she saw a lovely garden. She wanted to go there, but she could not fit through the opening.

Then Alice noticed a bottle marked “DRINK ME.” She checked it carefully and found no warning. After one drink, she began to shrink. Soon she was small enough for the little door, but she had left the key on the table above her. She could not reach it. A cake marked “EAT ME” made her grow very tall. Now the key was close, but the doorway was far too small.

Alice felt confused and began to cry. Her tears formed a pool on the floor. She was changing size again and trying to understand the strange rules of this place. The rabbit hole had brought her somewhere that seemed like a dream, but every new choice created a new problem. Alice waited. Alice waited.

B1.text:
While sitting beside her sister, Alice noticed a white rabbit wearing a waistcoat. It glanced at a watch and hurried away, saying it was late. Alice had never seen a rabbit carry a watch, so she followed it across a field and into a hole. The passage descended farther than she expected. As she fell, she passed shelves and pictures and wondered what would happen when she reached the bottom.

Alice landed in a long room with doors on every side. They were locked, but a small glass table held a golden key. She discovered that it opened a very small door. Beyond the doorway was a beautiful garden. Alice wanted to enter, yet she was much too large to pass through.

A bottle marked “DRINK ME” stood nearby. Alice looked for a warning and found none. She drank a little and shrank until the garden door seemed possible. Then she saw that she had left the key on the table, now far above her. A small cake marked “EAT ME” made her grow again. This time she was so tall that the doorway could not help her.

Alice felt trapped by the changes. She cried, and her tears spread across the floor, making a pool around her. She could not predict what would happen next or which choice would help. The room’s strange objects seemed to invite her forward while also making her task harder. Alice had begun by following a curious rabbit; now she needed to learn how this unfamiliar world worked before she could reach the garden.

title: The Pool of Tears
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Alice grew so tall that her head touched the ceiling. She felt unhappy and cried again. Soon the room filled with water from her tears. When she began to shrink, she slipped into the pool and swam toward a dry place. She met a mouse in the water and tried to speak politely. The mouse was not pleased when she mentioned cats, so Alice changed the subject.

More animals joined them. They included a duck, a dodo, a lory, and an eaglet. They all needed to get out of the water. On the bank, the dodo announced that they should hold a race to dry themselves. There was no starting line, and everyone ran whenever they liked. They ran around in a circle until they were dry.

The dodo said that the race was over and asked who had won. The group could not agree. The dodo decided that everyone had won. Alice gave each animal a small sweet from her pocket as a prize. She had no idea whether the rules made sense, but the animals were pleased.

The mouse began to tell a story about a dog and a person who disliked cats. Alice tried to listen, yet she kept thinking about Dinah, her own cat. She mentioned Dinah’s hunting, and the animals became nervous. They slowly left Alice alone. She had meant to share a familiar thought, but it reminded her new friends of something they feared. Alice continued toward the garden, now wondering how easily a careless word could change a conversation.

Alice’s tears made a pool across the floor. As she became smaller, she fell into the water and swam toward the edge. A mouse was swimming nearby. Alice tried to start a friendly conversation, but when she spoke about cats, the mouse became upset. She apologized and changed the topic.

Other animals arrived in the pool: a duck, a dodo, a lory, and an eaglet. They were all wet and wanted to dry themselves. The dodo proposed a race on the bank. There were no clear rules. The animals began running in different directions and stopped when they felt dry. The dodo then declared that everyone had won. Alice gave each of them a sweet from her pocket as a prize.

Afterward, the mouse offered to tell a serious story about a dog and a person who disliked cats. Alice tried to pay attention, but she kept thinking about Dinah, her own cat. She described Dinah’s skill at catching mice. The other animals heard this as a warning and became frightened. One by one, they moved away from Alice.

Alice had not wanted to scare anyone. She was learning that a familiar subject could feel very different to someone else. Even though the animals had shared an unusual adventure, they did not yet know one another well. Alice continued by herself, hoping to reach the garden. The experience left her with a small lesson about conversation: listening matters, and a careless comment can end a friendly meeting before it really begins.

title: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After climbing out of the pool, Alice and the animals stood on the bank. They were cold and wet. The dodo suggested a race to help them dry. He marked no starting point and gave no clear directions. The animals ran around the shore in many different ways. After a while, the dodo stopped them and announced that the race was finished.

The animals asked who had won. The dodo thought for a long time and said that everyone was a winner. Alice liked this answer. She had a few small sweets in her pocket and gave one to each animal as a prize. They thanked her, and for a moment the group felt cheerful.

The mouse then offered to tell a story. He wanted to explain why he was annoyed with a dog and a person. Alice tried to listen carefully. The mouse told it in a serious way, but Alice could not follow all of it. She asked questions and sometimes thought of other things. When she mentioned Dinah, her cat, the animals became uncomfortable. Alice praised Dinah for catching mice, and the mouse hurried away.

Alice had not meant to be rude. She had simply forgotten that the animals might fear the animal she loved. Once they left, she felt alone again. The race had been fun because everyone could join, but the story showed how difficult it could be to understand someone from a different life. Alice continued her journey and tried to pay closer attention to what others were saying.

B1.text:
Once Alice and the animals reached the bank, they were soaked and shivering. The dodo proposed a race, believing that movement would dry them. He made no track and explained no rules. The animals ran around the shore whenever they chose, so there was no obvious beginning or end. Eventually the dodo called them back and announced that the race was over.

They asked who had won. After considering the question, the dodo declared that everyone should receive a prize. Alice agreed and handed out small sweets she had saved in her pocket. The animals were pleased, and the strange contest ended happily even though nobody had followed a shared plan.

The mouse offered to tell a story about a dog and a person who disliked cats. Alice tried to listen, but she found the story difficult to follow. She interrupted with questions and sometimes let her thoughts wander. Then she began talking about Dinah, her own cat, and explained that Dinah was good at catching mice. The animals heard this as a frightening reminder of danger. The mouse left, and the others soon followed.

Alice had meant to talk about someone she loved, not to threaten her new companions. She began to understand that the same subject can feel pleasant to one person and worrying to another. The race had brought the group together for a moment, while the conversation revealed how little they knew about each other. Alice felt lonely again, but she also had a reason to listen more carefully as she continued through Wonderland.

title: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Alice reached a small house and met the White Rabbit again. He thought she was his servant, Mary Ann, and ordered her to fetch his gloves and a fan. Alice went inside because she was curious and wanted to understand what was happening. She found the gloves and fan in a room upstairs. She picked up the fan, and soon she began to feel a familiar change: she was growing.

Alice grew so large that her body filled much of the little house. She could no longer stand comfortably. The White Rabbit looked through the window and became frightened. He called for help. A lizard named Bill was sent down the chimney to discover what was inside. Alice pushed him away with her foot, and he flew out of the chimney. The animals outside ran about in confusion.

The rabbit and his helpers tried to get Alice out. They threw small stones through the window. The stones changed into little cakes when they landed. Alice ate one and began to shrink. When she became small enough, she ran out of the house and escaped into the garden.

Outside, Alice found herself among tall plants and strange paths. A large puppy came toward her, playful but much bigger than she was. Alice used a stick to distract it and then moved away safely. She continued on, unsure which path would lead to the garden. The rabbit had treated her like a servant, but Alice had learned that following someone’s orders without understanding them could place her in a difficult situation.

B1.text:
At a small house, Alice met the White Rabbit. He mistook her for his servant and told her to bring his gloves and fan. Alice went inside, partly because she wanted to help and partly because she was curious. She found the objects upstairs. After picking up the fan, she began to grow again. The rooms were far too small for her changing body.

The White Rabbit looked in through a window and panicked. He called for help. His servant Bill, a lizard, was sent down the chimney to investigate. Alice pushed him away, and Bill came flying out. The animals gathered outside were confused and frightened by the enormous girl inside the house.

The rabbit’s helpers tried several ways to remove Alice. They threw small stones through the window. As they landed near her, the stones became little cakes. Alice ate one and started to shrink. When she was small enough, she escaped from the house and reached the garden.

She soon encountered a puppy that was playful but huge beside her. Alice used a stick to distract it and moved out of its way. The encounter reminded her that even a friendly creature could be dangerous when there was such a difference in size. Alice continued along the garden paths, still unsure where she was going. The rabbit had assumed she would obey him, and she had acted before asking what he meant. Her choices had brought her into a tight situation. Now she was learning to pause, notice what was happening, and find a way out.

title: The Cyclone
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dorothy lived on a farm in Kansas with her uncle, her aunt, and a little dog named Toto. The land was flat, and the sky often looked gray. One afternoon, a cyclone began to blow. Dorothy heard her aunt and uncle calling for her to reach the storm shelter. She ran outside, but Toto hid under the bed. When Dorothy pulled him out, the house lifted into the air.

The cyclone carried the house far above the ground. Dorothy and Toto felt the house turn and move, but they were not hurt. Dorothy looked out of the window and saw clouds passing by. At last the house came down with a bump. Dorothy opened the door and found a bright, colorful country. The grass was green, and flowers grew everywhere.

A group of little people came to meet her. Their leader thanked Dorothy because the house had landed on the Wicked Witch of the East and freed them. Dorothy was surprised. She had not meant to hurt anyone; she only wanted to get out of the storm. The people gave her the witch’s silver shoes and said she should ask the great Wizard of Oz for help.

Dorothy wanted to return to Kansas. The people told her that the Wizard lived in the Emerald City, far along a yellow road. She began the journey with Toto. A2.text:
Dorothy lived on a farm in Kansas with her uncle, her aunt, and a little dog named Toto. The land was flat, and the sky often looked gray. One afternoon, a cyclone began to blow. Dorothy heard her aunt and uncle calling for her to reach the storm shelter. She ran outside, but Toto hid under the bed. When Dorothy pulled him out, the house lifted into the air.

The cyclone carried the house far above the ground. Dorothy and Toto felt the house turn and move, but they were not hurt. Dorothy looked out of the window and saw clouds passing by. At last the house came down with a bump. Dorothy opened the door and found a bright, colorful country. The grass was green, and flowers grew everywhere.

A group of little people came to meet her. Their leader thanked Dorothy because the house had landed on the Wicked Witch of the East and freed them. Dorothy was surprised. She had not meant to hurt anyone; she only wanted to get out of the storm. The people gave her the witch’s silver shoes and said she should ask the great Wizard of Oz for help.

Dorothy wanted to return to Kansas. The people told her that the Wizard lived in the Emerald City, far along a yellow road. She began the journey with Toto. Dorothy did not know the country or its rules, but she decided to follow the road and ask for help. She missed her aunt and uncle, and Toto stayed close beside her. Dorothy wanted to know what the new country was like, but she also wanted a clear path back home.

B1.text:
Dorothy lived with her aunt and uncle on a Kansas farm. Her only close companion was Toto, a small dog. One afternoon, a cyclone came toward the farm. Dorothy heard her relatives call her to the shelter, but Toto had hidden beneath a bed. She carried him outside, and the wind lifted the house before she could reach safety.

The house spun through the air while Dorothy and Toto held on. They were frightened, but the strong house protected them. After a long journey, it landed with a sudden shake. When Dorothy opened the door, she saw a vivid country unlike the gray landscape she knew. Green grass and flowers surrounded the house.

Small people approached. Their leader explained that Dorothy’s house had landed on the Wicked Witch of the East, ending the witch’s control over them. Dorothy was shocked; she had not chosen to fight anyone. The grateful people gave her a pair of silver shoes that had belonged to the witch. They advised her to travel to the Emerald City and ask the Wizard of Oz to send her home.

Dorothy wanted Kansas and her family, so she agreed to go. The route began along a yellow road. She started walking with Toto, unsure what she would find. The cyclone had carried her into a strange land, and now she had to make choices without knowing its customs. She hoped that the Wizard could help, but the journey itself would bring new companions and tests. The color and beauty of the new country amazed Dorothy. She missed her family, but Toto was beside her, and she decided to find someone who could explain where she had landed.

title: The Council with the Munchkins
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dorothy stood with Toto among the Munchkins. Their leader explained that the Wicked Witch of the East had controlled them for a long time. Dorothy’s house had landed on the witch, and the silver shoes now belonged to Dorothy. The Munchkins were happy to be free, but Dorothy felt worried. She had not meant to arrive in this country or become part of a fight between witches.

The people told her that another witch, the Wicked Witch of the West, was still powerful. Dorothy wanted to go back to Kansas. The Munchkins could not take her there, so they suggested she ask the Wizard of Oz. He lived in the Emerald City. The road to the city was marked with yellow bricks. Dorothy decided to follow it and take Toto with her.

Before she left, the Munchkins gave Dorothy a welcome and thanked her. The good Witch of the North placed a protective mark on her forehead. She also warned Dorothy not to remove the silver shoes. They might help her on the journey. Dorothy did not understand how important they were, but she kept them on.

At last Dorothy stepped onto the road. She was a visitor in a place she did not understand, but the Munchkins had treated her kindly. She knew she could not return to Kansas alone, so she began walking toward the Emerald City. She hoped the Wizard would know how to send her home. The road was the first clear direction she had received. Dorothy hoped the Emerald City would bring answers, and she kept the silver shoes safe as she walked away from the Munchkins.

B1.text:
The Munchkins gathered around Dorothy after the house landed. Their leader explained that the Wicked Witch of the East had ruled them. By landing on the witch, Dorothy had freed them. They were grateful, though Dorothy herself was unsettled. She had not planned to challenge a witch; she had only been caught in a storm.

The people told Dorothy that the Wicked Witch of the West remained dangerous. Dorothy wanted to return to Kansas, but the Munchkins did not know how to take her there. They recommended asking the Wizard of Oz, who lived in the Emerald City. To reach him, she could follow a road made of yellow bricks. Dorothy decided to try this route with Toto beside her.

Before she began, the people welcomed her and thanked her. The Good Witch of the North touched Dorothy’s forehead, leaving a protective mark. She also advised Dorothy to keep the silver shoes she had received from the witch of the East. Dorothy did not yet know what the shoes could do, but she followed the advice.

When Dorothy started along the road, she was leaving the only people she had met in this strange country. The Munchkins had helped her, and their kindness made her feel less alone. Still, she had a long way to go and no guarantee that the Wizard would grant her wish. She chose to keep moving because a chance of getting home was better than staying where she was. The yellow road gave Dorothy a practical next step. She had no map of the strange country, so she chose to trust the Munchkins’ directions and continue toward the city.

title: How Dorothy Saved the Scarecrow
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
As Dorothy walked along the yellow road, she passed a scarecrow standing in a field. He was made of straw and wore old clothes. His head was stuffed with straw, and a painted face showed a friendly smile. Dorothy was surprised when the scarecrow spoke. He said that he could not move because he was tied to a pole.

Dorothy climbed onto a fence and carefully lifted him down. The scarecrow felt happy to be free. He told her that he had no brain and wished he could think better. Dorothy explained that she was going to the Emerald City to ask the Wizard to help her return to Kansas. The scarecrow asked if he could come along and ask the Wizard for a brain.

Dorothy agreed. She thought that traveling with a friend would be better than walking alone. The scarecrow did not know much about the world, but he asked thoughtful questions. He wanted to understand how things worked. Dorothy and Toto told him about the farm and the storm. As they walked, they became a team.

The road led them through a wood. They took turns helping each other when the path was difficult. The scarecrow could see far ahead because he was tall, while Dorothy could solve ordinary problems. They believed the Wizard might help them both. Dorothy wanted a way home; the scarecrow wanted the ability to think. They continued toward the Emerald City together. The scarecrow thanked her again, and Toto walked around them. Dorothy felt less lonely with another traveler beside her. The Emerald City now seemed like a shared destination.

title: The Road Through the Forest
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dorothy and the Scarecrow continued along the yellow road. The bricks became rough, uneven, and sometimes missing. The Scarecrow did not notice the holes. He stepped into them and fell, so Dorothy had to lift him back onto his feet. He laughed because he could not feel pain. At noon they rested beside a brook. Dorothy ate bread from her basket, but the Scarecrow did not need food because his mouth was only painted.

After lunch, the Scarecrow asked Dorothy about Kansas. She told him that the cyclone had carried her away and that the land at home was gray and dry. The Scarecrow had no brains, but he was curious about the world.

He told Dorothy how a farmer had made him only two days earlier. The farmer painted his face, filled his clothes with straw, and put him on a pole in a cornfield. The Scarecrow tried to walk away but could not touch the ground. Crows came to eat the corn because they knew he was only stuffed with straw. He began to wish for brains so he could think and understand things.

They walked on until the road entered a large, dark forest. The Scarecrow said they should follow it because it must lead somewhere. Dorothy held his arm when she could not see. He spotted a small cottage, and they went inside. Dorothy slept on a bed of dry leaves while the Scarecrow stood watch until morning.

B1.text:
The yellow road became rough after Dorothy and the Scarecrow had walked for several hours. Some bricks were uneven, broken, or missing. Dorothy and Toto went around the holes, but the Scarecrow walked straight ahead and repeatedly fell. He could not feel pain, so he laughed while Dorothy helped him stand again. At midday they rested beside a brook. Dorothy ate bread from her basket, while the Scarecrow explained that he could not eat because his mouth was painted and his head was filled with straw.

The Scarecrow asked Dorothy about Kansas. She described the gray prairie and explained that a cyclone had carried her away. He could not understand why she wanted to leave the beautiful land around them. Dorothy told him that people often prefer their own homes, even when another place seems more attractive. The Scarecrow listened and then told her about his short life.

A farmer had made him only two days before. He painted the Scarecrow’s face, filled his clothes with straw, and placed him on a pole to frighten birds away from the corn. The Scarecrow tried to follow the farmer but could not reach the ground. Crows discovered that he was not real and ate the corn beside him. He felt useless and wished for a brain, believing that it would help him understand and act wisely.

By evening, Dorothy and the Scarecrow reached a forest where the branches covered the road. They continued in the dark. Dorothy held the Scarecrow’s arm because she could not see, while he searched for somewhere to rest. He found a small cottage. Dorothy slept on dry leaves, and the tireless Scarecrow stood quietly in a corner until morning.

title: Peter Breaks Through
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
The Darling children lived with their parents and a dog named Nana. Wendy often told stories to John and Michael. Peter Pan had listened from outside their window. One night he came into the nursery, hoping Wendy would tell him more. Peter could fly, but he had lost his shadow in the room.

Peter tried to catch it, but the shadow would not stay. Wendy woke and found him struggling. She was surprised, yet she helped him by sewing it back onto his feet. Peter was pleased and told her about Neverland, where he lived with the Lost Boys. He said fairies could help people fly if they believed and had happy thoughts.

Wendy and her brothers wanted to hear more. Peter offered to take them to the island. Wendy liked stories about faraway places, but she knew that leaving home was a serious choice. The nursery was safe and familiar, and their parents were nearby. Peter waited while they thought about the invitation.

Peter seemed friendly, but he had entered their room without asking. Wendy had to consider whether his exciting story was enough reason to trust him. She also had to think about John and Michael, who looked to her for advice. The open window led toward a new adventure, but the children could not be sure what waited outside. Before following Peter, Wendy knew that she should ask her brothers what they wanted. John and Michael were excited, but they also depended on her. The family had a home, regular meals, and adults who looked after them. Neverland might be wonderful, yet it was still unknown. She tried to balance curiosity with care.

The Darling family lived with Nana, a dog who watched over the children. Wendy told stories to John and Michael. Peter Pan had listened from outside their window. One night he entered the nursery, hoping Wendy would tell him more. He could fly, but he had misplaced his shadow in the room.

Peter tried to catch it, but it would not remain attached. Wendy woke and found him struggling. Although she was surprised, she helped by sewing the shadow back onto him. The window opened onto possibility and uncertainty. A new adventure might be exciting, but the children could not know what was waiting outside or whether they could return easily. Peter’s offer sounded exciting, but Wendy understood that a new place could not be judged from a story alone. She needed to consider safety, her brothers’ feelings, and the family they would leave behind. Their decision would affect all three children, so she wanted to think rather than follow Peter immediately.

title: The Shadow
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
After Wendy sewed Peter’s shadow back in place, he told her about Neverland. The Lost Boys lived there without parents. They had made a home among the island’s forests and hidden places. Wendy wondered whether they missed having a family.

Peter said that he had come because he liked listening to Wendy’s stories. He thought she could tell stories to the Lost Boys and help make their home more comfortable. Wendy liked the idea of helping them, though she was not sure that it was her responsibility. John and Michael also wanted to travel with Peter.

Peter showed them how to fly. He said that happy thoughts and fairy dust would lift them. The children tried, and soon they rose above the floor. Wendy looked down at the nursery. She knew that flying through the window meant leaving a place she knew for a place she had never seen.

Wendy chose to go, and her brothers followed. Together they flew toward Neverland. She wondered whether the Lost Boys would feel like a family and whether she could care for them without forgetting her own family at home. Wendy knew that helping the boys could be kind, but she had to learn more before she promised anything. She cared about her brothers and her parents too. The nursery was a place where they were known and protected. Neverland might become a home, but it could not do so in one night. She wanted to help, but she would decide after learning what the boys truly needed.

title: Come Away, Come Away!
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Wendy, John, and Michael flew after Peter through the night. They crossed over rooftops and traveled farther than they had gone before without an adult. Peter moved quickly, and the children tried to stay together. They became tired but were excited to see Neverland.

Peter told them that the Lost Boys lived on the island. He also warned them about Captain Hook and the pirates. The island was not only a place for games; it could be dangerous. Wendy wanted to meet the boys, but she also wanted to know how the children would stay safe.

Below them, the island came into view. Wendy saw forests and water and heard distant sounds. Peter flew ahead because he knew the way. Wendy, John, and Michael were visitors, so they depended on him for directions. Wendy wondered whether Peter understood how frightening the journey could feel to someone new.

They continued toward land. The children were far from home and had no easy way back. Wendy stayed close to her brothers. She hoped to help the Lost Boys, but first she needed to understand the island and its rules. Exploring felt exciting, yet she knew they would need to watch out for one another. They kept a steady distance from Peter so no one was left behind. Wendy thought about how much they relied on him, since he alone knew the way. She planned to ask questions when they arrived and to keep her brothers together. The island was a story becoming real, but they still needed care.

B1.text:
Wendy, John, and Michael followed Peter through the night sky. They passed over familiar streets and traveled farther than they had ever gone without an adult. Peter knew the route and moved quickly, so the children kept close to avoid becoming separated. They were tired, but the promise of Neverland kept them going.

Peter described the island’s residents. The Lost Boys would be there, but Captain Hook and his pirates could also be nearby. Wendy realized the trip was not simply a game. New places could bring danger as well as excitement. She wanted to meet the boys but needed to know how they could stay safe.

At last they saw the island below. Forests and water stretched into the distance, and unfamiliar sounds rose toward them. Peter was confident because he knew the place. Wendy and her brothers depended on him for directions, and Wendy wondered whether he understood that newcomers might be afraid.

They continued toward shore. They had left home and could not easily return. Wendy stayed close to John and Michael. She wanted to help the Lost Boys, but she first needed to learn the island’s rules and decide how much to trust Peter. The children were brave, though they still needed guidance and care. The children were relying on Peter, who knew the route but did not share their experience of being new. Wendy watched John and Michael and tried to keep them close. She understood that exploring was easier when the group stayed together. Once they landed, she would ask what rules and dangers they should know.

title: The Flight
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Peter led Wendy, John, and Michael toward Neverland. He gave them a strange direction: second to the right, then straight on until morning. The children tried to follow, although the way was hard to understand. They flew over the sea for a long time. On the second sea they reached their third night, and they began to feel cold and hungry. Peter chased birds and brought food to them. Still, he often rushed away because he wanted to have more adventures.

The journey made the children sleepy. Michael started to fall through the air, but Peter caught him just in time. Wendy was frightened and angry. Peter had not been watching the children closely. He taught them to float and sleep in a strong wind, then disappeared again to explore. Wendy and her brothers continued without knowing when he would return.

After many days and nights, they finally reached the island. It looked dark and dangerous from above. Peter pointed toward places where the Lost Boys lived and told them that Captain Hook and his pirates were there too. Wendy wanted to see the island, but she also thought about the home and parents they had left. She stayed close to John and Michael. They had arrived, but they still needed to understand the island and decide how to keep one another safe. The children could hear the wind around them. Wendy watched the boys and tried to remember the direction they had come from. She wanted to help her brothers, even when Peter was not nearby.

B1.text:
Peter gave Wendy, John, and Michael directions to Neverland: second to the right and straight on until morning. The route was difficult to follow, but they flew on. They crossed several seas, and by the third night over the second sea they were cold and hungry. Peter chased birds and brought the children food. He was quick and excited, but he also kept leaving them to follow his own adventures.

The long flight made everyone tired. Michael began to drop through the air while he slept. Peter caught him at the last moment. Wendy was upset that Peter had not been watching him. Peter showed the children how to float and sleep safely in a strong wind. Then he went away again. The others had to continue without knowing when he would come back.

Many days and nights passed before the island appeared below them. From above, it seemed dark and threatening. Peter pointed out where the Lost Boys might be and spoke about Captain Hook and his pirates. Wendy had wanted an adventure, but she now understood that the island could be dangerous. She missed the familiar nursery and her parents, and she kept John and Michael close. They had reached the place Peter called home, but they were newcomers. They would need to learn its dangers and care for one another instead of depending only on Peter. The children could hear the wind around them. Wendy watched the boys and tried to remember the direction they had come from. She wanted to help her brothers, even when Peter was not nearby.

title: A Scandal in Bohemia
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Dr. Watson visited his old friend Sherlock Holmes and found him speaking with a masked man. The visitor was the King of Bohemia. He feared that a photograph of him with Irene Adler could damage his reputation and his planned marriage. He asked Holmes to find the picture before Irene used it.

Holmes studied Irene’s habits and watched her house. He disguised himself as a worker and learned where she kept her important things. Watson helped him create a small distraction outside. When smoke seemed to come from the house, Irene hurried to a hiding place for the photograph. Holmes noticed exactly where she went.

Holmes returned later with Watson to take the picture. But Irene had already understood that he was watching her. She had disguised herself and followed him. She told Holmes that she had kept the photograph only to protect herself. She did not plan to harm the King unless he threatened her.

Irene left the country with the photograph. Holmes could not recover it, but the King was safe from public embarrassment. He offered Holmes a valuable ring, yet Holmes asked instead for Irene’s photograph. He admired how she had understood his plan and acted before he could. Watson saw that intelligence can belong to the person being investigated as well as the detective. Holmes accepted that Irene had protected herself. The King wanted the picture removed, but the solution did not give him control over her choices. Watson respected the detective’s judgment. Watson considered what she had done.

Holmes investigated Irene’s routine and studied the house. He disguised himself as a worker to observe her movements. Watson helped create a commotion outside. When smoke appeared to rise from the building, Irene ran to a hidden place for the photograph. Holmes saw where she kept it and believed he could retrieve it later.

However, Irene had recognized that Holmes was paying attention. She changed her appearance and followed him after he left. She told him that she kept the photograph as protection, not as a plan to harm the King. If he respected her privacy, she would not use it against him. She then left the country with the image.

Holmes had solved where the photograph was hidden but had not predicted Irene’s response. The King escaped the embarrassment he feared, though the photograph remained beyond his reach. He offered Holmes a valuable reward. Holmes asked for Irene’s picture instead, respecting her intelligence and the way she had anticipated his strategy. Watson understood that a detective’s cleverness does not guarantee control over another person’s choices. Holmes understood that finding the photograph did not mean he owned the decision. Irene had kept it to defend herself. The King’s worry was solved, but her actions deserved respect too.

title: The Red-Headed League
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Jabez Wilson, a shopkeeper with bright red hair, came to Holmes with a strange story. A group called the Red-Headed League had paid him to copy an encyclopedia every day. The work was easy, and the pay was good. Then one morning he arrived and found a notice saying the League had ended.

Holmes asked questions about Wilson’s shop and his assistant, Vincent Spaulding. Spaulding was willing to work for very little money and often disappeared into the cellar. Holmes looked at the assistant’s trousers and noticed marks on the knees. He also checked the bank near Wilson’s shop and learned that a safe was being kept there.

Holmes guessed that the League had been invented to keep Wilson away from his shop. While Wilson sat copying in another room, someone could dig a tunnel from the cellar toward the bank. Holmes and the police hid near the bank one evening. They waited until two men came through the tunnel. One was Spaulding, whose real name was John Clay.

Holmes and the police caught the men before they could rob the bank. Wilson had believed he was doing an odd but harmless job. In fact, the job had been used to distract him. Holmes showed that small details, like dirty knees and unusual working hours, could reveal a larger plan. Holmes explained his conclusion to Wilson. The shopkeeper had not been foolish to accept work, but he had not asked enough questions. He now understood why the job had ended so suddenly.

B1.text:
Jabez Wilson, a shopkeeper known for his bright red hair, asked Holmes about a job that had suddenly disappeared. The Red-Headed League had paid him to copy an encyclopedia for several hours each day. The work seemed simple and the wages were surprisingly good. One morning, he found a note saying the organization had closed.

Holmes asked about Wilson’s shop and his assistant, Vincent Spaulding. Spaulding accepted unusually low pay and often went into the cellar. Holmes noticed dirt on the assistant’s knees. He also learned that a bank was close to the shop and held a valuable safe.

Holmes suspected that the League had been created to keep Wilson away from his business. While Wilson copied text in another room, someone could dig from the cellar toward the bank. Holmes and the police waited there one night. Two men emerged through the tunnel. One was Spaulding, whose real identity was John Clay.

The police arrested them before they could rob the bank. Wilson had assumed the copying job was strange but harmless. Holmes showed him that its purpose was to occupy his time while the thieves worked. The solution depended on connecting details that seemed unrelated: the easy job, the assistant’s low wages, his long absences, and the dirt on his clothes. A careful observer could see the plan hidden inside ordinary events. A good wage, a strange schedule, and the assistant’s habits made more sense when Holmes connected them to the nearby bank. Careful observation made the plan visible.

title: A Case of Identity
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
Mary Sutherland came to Holmes because her fiancé, Hosmer Angel, had disappeared. She explained that Hosmer had been kind and careful. He asked her to write letters to him and said she should keep their engagement private. On the morning they planned to marry, he entered a carriage and vanished before it reached the church.

Holmes asked about Mary’s family. Her stepfather, James Windibank, did not want her to marry. He often traveled for work and had discouraged her from going out. Holmes noticed that Hosmer never met Mary in daylight and that his voice and appearance were unusual. He compared the letters and found that they had been typed.

Holmes realized that Hosmer Angel was not a real person. Windibank had disguised himself as Mary’s fiancé to keep her from meeting other men while he was away. He wanted Mary to remain at home because her money helped support the family. When he returned from travel, the disguise could disappear without explanation.

Holmes told Mary what he believed had happened. She was hurt, but she said she would continue waiting for Hosmer. Holmes warned that the man had chosen to deceive her. The mystery was solved, yet Mary still had to decide what to do with the truth. Mary had trusted the person she thought she knew. Holmes could explain the trick, but he could not choose how she would respond. The truth could be painful even when it was clear. Mary would need time to think. Mary listened.

B1.text:
Mary Sutherland asked Holmes to find her fiancé, Hosmer Angel, who had vanished on the morning of their wedding. She described him as gentle and dependable. He had insisted that they keep the engagement secret and asked her to write letters because he could not always speak freely. At the church, he entered a carriage and disappeared before they arrived.

Holmes asked about Mary’s home life. Her stepfather, James Windibank, opposed her marriage and often traveled for work. Holmes found it unusual that Hosmer never met Mary in daylight. His voice and appearance also seemed carefully controlled. The letters Mary had received were typed, which made it harder to identify the writer.

Holmes concluded that Hosmer did not exist. Windibank had used a disguise to pose as Mary’s fiancé. He wanted her to remain unmarried and at home because her income supported the household. When his work trips ended, he could simply disappear as Hosmer and return as himself.

Holmes explained the deception to Mary. She was distressed but said she would wait for Hosmer. Holmes warned her that the man who had vanished was the same person who had lied to her. The case had an answer, but a solution could not decide Mary’s next step for her. She would need to choose whether to accept the truth and challenge the person who had deceived her. Holmes uncovered Windibank’s identity, but Mary still had control over what she did next. She had to decide whether hope was stronger than the evidence and how to protect herself.

title: The Boscombe Valley Mystery
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A young man named James McCarthy was accused of killing his father in a valley. The father had been found dead near a pool, and people believed James had argued with him. James said he was innocent. His fiancée, Alice Turner, asked Holmes to investigate because she did not believe he was guilty.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A lion was sleeping in the shade when a small mouse ran across his paw. The lion woke and caught the mouse. He was angry that such a tiny animal had disturbed him. The mouse begged to be released. It promised that one day it might help the lion. The lion laughed because he could not imagine needing help from a mouse. Still, he opened his paw and let the little animal go.

Some time later, hunters came into the forest. They set a strong net to catch the lion. The lion stepped into it and became trapped. He roared loudly and pulled at the ropes, but the net held him. The mouse heard his cries and hurried over.

The mouse remembered the lion’s kindness. It began to gnaw through the ropes with its sharp teeth. The work took time, but at last the net opened enough for the lion to escape. The lion thanked the mouse. He understood that even a very small animal could do something important.

The two animals had helped each other in different ways. The lion had been strong enough to catch the mouse, but the mouse had been small enough to reach and cut the ropes. Their story shows that kindness may return in an unexpected form. A person should not decide that someone is useless because they are small or seem weak. The lion had not expected a mouse to matter, yet the mouse remembered the choice he had made. Their different abilities were useful at different times. The lion could be generous, and the mouse could be brave.

B1.text:
A lion slept beneath a tree. A mouse ran over his paw and woke him. The lion caught the mouse and wanted to punish it for disturbing his rest. The mouse asked to be set free and promised that it might repay the lion one day. The lion thought this was funny: a small mouse could hardly help a powerful lion. But he chose to release it.

Later, hunters placed a net in the forest. The lion walked into it and became trapped. He pulled hard, but the ropes held him. His loud roars reached the mouse, which came to see what had happened. The mouse remembered that the lion had spared its life.

It started biting the ropes with its small teeth. It worked patiently until the net opened. The lion was able to get free and thanked the mouse. He now understood that strength was not the only way to help someone. The mouse was too small to fight the hunters, but it could reach the ropes and cut them apart.

The lion had once believed that he could never need a mouse. The experience changed his view. The mouse’s kindness and skill mattered more than its size. The fable suggests that a generous action can bring help later, even from someone we did not expect. It also warns against judging another creature only by its appearance or power. The story gives both animals a chance to help. The lion first chooses mercy, and the mouse later shows courage. Each learns that a small act can matter more than someone expects.

title: The Wolf and the Lamb
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A lamb was drinking from a clear stream. A wolf stood farther up the water. He saw the lamb and wanted an excuse to attack it. The wolf shouted that the lamb was making the water dirty. The lamb answered politely that it was drinking downstream, so it could not be sending mud toward the wolf.

The wolf then said that the lamb had insulted him the year before. The lamb explained that it was not yet born at that time. The wolf changed his complaint again. He said that if the lamb had not done it, one of its relatives must have. The lamb could not answer for someone else.

The wolf did not listen to the lamb’s reasonable replies. He had already decided what he wanted to do. The accusations were not true, but he used them to make his behavior sound fair. The lamb had no power to stop him. The wolf carried out his plan despite the facts.

The story shows that a person can make many claims without having evidence. A fair argument should consider what happened and what each person could have done. The wolf used his greater strength to ignore the truth. The lamb tried to explain, but the wolf was not interested in an honest answer. The fable asks readers to notice when someone is using excuses to hide an unfair choice. The lamb answered carefully and did not insult the wolf. Its logic could not change the wolf’s decision, because the wolf was not trying to learn what was true.

B1.text:
A lamb came to drink from a stream. A wolf stood upstream and wanted to catch it. He accused the lamb of making the water muddy. The lamb calmly explained that the water flowed from the wolf toward the lamb, so it could not have dirtied the wolf’s drinking place.

The wolf made a new accusation. He said that the lamb had spoken badly about him the previous year. The lamb pointed out that it had not been born then. The wolf changed the story again, claiming that a member of the lamb’s family must have insulted him. The lamb said it could not be responsible for something a relative might have done.

The wolf ignored every answer. He had chosen to attack and was only inventing reasons afterward. The lamb had no way to make the wolf listen or to defend itself against the stronger animal. The wolf used false arguments to make an unfair act appear justified.

The fable warns that a person who wants to do harm may keep changing the accusation when the first claim is disproved. Evidence and careful reasoning matter, but they cannot persuade someone who refuses to be fair. Readers can compare the wolf’s claims with the lamb’s simple explanations and see that the real problem is not the water. The wolf’s power lets him ignore the truth. Readers can see the difference between an honest question and an excuse. The wolf changes his claims whenever the lamb answers, which shows that he does not want a fair discussion.

title: The Ass and the Grasshopper
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
An ass heard a grasshopper singing in the field. The music sounded light and beautiful. The ass asked what the grasshopper ate to make such a lovely song. The grasshopper said that it lived on dew, the tiny drops of water found on leaves in the morning.

The ass believed that the grasshopper’s food must be the reason for its music. It decided to eat only dew. The ass stopped eating the food it needed and waited for drops of water instead. At first it felt proud of copying the grasshopper. It hoped that it would soon sing in the same way.

But an ass is much larger than a grasshopper and needs different food. The dew did not give the ass enough strength. It became weak and could not keep working as before. It had copied the grasshopper without asking whether the same choice would be healthy for its own body.

The grasshopper’s song came from its own nature; a change of diet could not simply give another animal the same ability. The ass learned that people and animals have different needs. It is unwise to copy a habit just because someone else seems successful. Before changing what we do, we should understand why the other person does it and whether the choice suits us. The ass could have asked whether dew provided enough food for a large animal. Instead, it copied what it saw and suffered. It needed to learn about its own body. Curiosity needs careful thinking.

title: The Wolf and the Crane
author: LessonCaptain (retelling)
summary:
A wolf ate too quickly and got a bone stuck in his throat. He could not remove it with his paws, and the bone hurt when he swallowed. The wolf asked the other animals to help, but they were afraid of his sharp teeth. A crane had a long beak and neck, so the wolf asked it to reach inside his mouth and take out the bone.

The crane was nervous. The wolf promised to give it a reward if it helped. The crane carefully put its beak into the wolf’s mouth and pulled the bone out. The wolf could breathe and eat again. The crane then asked for the promised payment.

The wolf replied that the crane should be glad to have taken its head out of his mouth safely. He refused to give a reward. The crane had helped the wolf, but it had trusted a promise from someone dangerous. The wolf treated the crane’s service as something it should have been grateful for, rather than keeping his word.

The fable asks readers to think about trust and fairness. Helping someone can be kind, but it is wise to consider the risk and the other person’s character. A promise matters only when the person who makes it chooses to keep it. The crane escaped unharmed, but it learned not to expect gratitude from someone who had shown no reason to be trusted. The crane used its skill to help, but it could not make the wolf keep his promise. It was fortunate to leave safely, and it could remember what had happened.

B1.text:
A wolf swallowed food too quickly, and a bone became stuck in his throat. He could not reach it with his paws, and it hurt him. The other animals were afraid to help because the wolf had dangerous teeth. He asked a crane, whose long beak could reach into his mouth, to remove the bone. The wolf promised a reward.

The crane hesitated. It understood the danger but decided to help. It carefully placed its beak in the wolf’s mouth and pulled out the bone. The wolf could breathe and eat normally again. The crane then asked for the payment he had promised.

The wolf refused. He said that the crane should be pleased simply to have escaped with its head. The crane had helped the wolf, but the wolf did not keep his word. He treated the successful rescue as a favor the crane should have been grateful to perform.

The story shows that helping can involve risk, especially when the other person has more power. The crane had a useful skill, yet it trusted a promise from an animal with a history of danger. The wolf’s behavior was unfair, and his refusal teaches the crane something about his character. A promise is not proof of trustworthiness by itself. Before helping, people can consider whether the person has shown honesty and whether there is a safer way to offer help. The crane had solved the wolf’s problem, but it could not demand fairness from an animal that refused to give it. Its experience offered a reason to be cautious next time.

title: The Old Buccaneer: Chapters I–VI
originalTitles: I. The Old Sea-dog at the Admiral Benbow
II. Black Dog Appears and Disappears
V. The Last of the Blind Man
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Jim Hawkins lives with his parents at the Admiral Benbow inn. One day, an old sailor called Billy Bones arrives with a heavy sea chest. He pays Jim to watch for a one-legged sailor, but he gives little explanation. Billy drinks heavily, frightens the guests with sea stories, and behaves rudely toward Jim’s father. Dr. Livesey warns Billy that his drinking is damaging his health and that his threats will have consequences.

A sailor named Black Dog later comes to the inn and asks for Billy. The two men argue and fight. Black Dog escapes, but Billy collapses after the struggle. Dr. Livesey treats him and warns him again about alcohol. Soon after, Billy receives a black spot, a warning from his former shipmates. Jim and his mother realize that the pirates may return. They search Billy’s room for money owed to the inn, but they do not take more than the debt. Jim finds a packet among Billy’s papers.

Blind Pew and other pirates arrive at night, searching for the packet. Jim and his mother escape with the papers just before the men surround the inn. Pew is knocked down during the pirates’ hurried escape and dies. Jim takes the packet to Dr. Livesey and Squire Trelawney. Inside, they find a map made by Captain Flint. It shows where the pirate’s treasure is buried. Trelawney decides to prepare a ship and sail for the island. Jim is excited, but he knows the map has already brought danger to his home.

 The adults around Jim do not all respond to danger in the same way. The doctor tries to stay calm and ask useful questions, while the squire is enthusiastic and sometimes careless. Captain Smollett is cautious because he must protect the whole crew. Jim watches these differences and slowly learns that confidence is not the same as good judgment. The map gives everyone a reason to travel, but it cannot tell them whom to trust. Billy Bones’s warnings, the black spot, and the sudden appearance of the hidden map have made ordinary life impossible. Jim’s courage grows through observation: he notices what adults miss, remembers important details, and shares information when it matters.

author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Jim travels to Bristol with Dr. Livesey and Squire Trelawney to join their ship, the Hispaniola. Trelawney has bought the vessel and hired its crew. At the Spy-glass inn, Jim meets Long John Silver, the one-legged cook. Silver is cheerful and helpful, and he knows many sailors. He tells Jim that he has not heard of the one-legged man Billy feared. Jim thinks Silver may be trustworthy.

Captain Smollett is less confident. He dislikes the crew’s attitudes, the way the ship is loaded, and the fact that people know their destination. He asks the squire to move the weapons and powder to a safer part of the ship. Trelawney is annoyed by the captain’s suspicion, but Dr. Livesey listens to the concerns. The Hispaniola sets sail for the island.

During the voyage, Jim sees that Silver works hard and treats the sailors warmly. But one night, while he is hidden in an apple barrel, Jim hears Silver talking with other crew members. Silver explains that he once served under Captain Flint and knows about the treasure. He is helping the honest passengers for now, but he plans to lead a mutiny after the treasure is found. Jim is shocked. He understands that Silver’s friendliness has concealed a dangerous plan.

Jim tells Captain Smollett, Dr. Livesey, and Squire Trelawney what he heard. They now know that many sailors are pirates. They cannot openly confront Silver because the crew could take control of the ship. Instead, they quietly identify the sailors they can trust and prepare to defend themselves. The island is near, and the voyage has become a contest of patience and planning.

 The ship carries more than passengers and supplies; it carries competing plans. Jim has not yet told the adults everything he heard, and each delay matters because the crew is approaching its destination. Captain Smollett’s concerns now seem less like bad temper and more like careful preparation. Dr. Livesey and Trelawney must work together even though they do not always agree. Jim sees how quickly a friendly conversation can change when someone has hidden intentions. The apple barrel gives him a safe place to listen, but what he learns makes him less safe afterward. He cannot solve the problem alone, so he brings the warning to the people who can plan. Their quiet response shows that careful teamwork may be more useful than a dramatic confrontation.

B2.text:
After Jim reaches Bristol, he joins Squire Trelawney and Dr. Livesey in preparing the Hispaniola. At the Spy-glass inn, he meets Long John Silver, the ship’s cook. Silver is lively and welcoming. He has one leg, but Jim does not connect him with Billy Bones’s warning because Silver seems so pleasant and helpful.

Captain Smollett distrusts the arrangements. The crew knows the ship’s destination, and the weapons and powder are not stored safely. Trelawney dislikes the captain’s criticism, but they move the arms as he requests. The Hispaniola sails, and Silver appears to be an excellent cook and popular leader among the sailors.

One night Jim climbs into an apple barrel to get a piece of fruit. From inside, he hears Silver speaking with several men. Silver reveals that he sailed with Captain Flint and knows the treasure story. He and his followers intend to wait until the treasure is found, then take it and seize the ship. The crew members have been pretending to be ordinary sailors. Jim realizes that Silver’s open, friendly manner is part of his disguise.

When Jim reports what he heard, the doctor, squire, and captain understand that they are outnumbered. They cannot arrest the mutineers without risking a fight on the ship. They decide to hide what they know and prepare quietly. The captain counts the people he can trust, keeps weapons ready, and looks for a safe moment to act. The treasure has brought them together, but it has also made the voyage dangerous before they have even reached land.

title: My Shore Adventure and the Stockade: Chapters XIII–XXI
originalTitles: XIII. How I Began My Shore Adventure
XV. The Man of the Island
XVI. How the Ship Was Abandoned
XVIII. End of the First Day’s Fighting
XIX. The Garrison in the Stockade
author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
When the Hispaniola reaches the island, the captain lets some sailors go ashore. Jim joins them, then slips away alone. In the woods, he sees Silver argue with a sailor who refuses to join the mutiny. Silver kills him, and Jim understands that the danger is real. Jim runs from the scene and meets Ben Gunn, a former pirate who has been stranded on the island for years. Ben says he knows where Flint’s treasure is and asks to be taken home.

Jim returns to his friends, who have moved into a wooden stockade. The doctor, squire, captain, and a few loyal sailors prepare for an attack. The doctor goes to speak with Silver, who offers a deal: give him the map and let his men take the ship, or face a fight. The captain refuses. Silver leaves, and the pirates attack the stockade. The defenders hold their position, although some people are injured and one of the loyal men dies.

Afterward, Jim leaves the stockade without telling the others. He finds Ben Gunn’s small boat and makes his way to the Hispaniola. The ship is no longer safely anchored. Jim boards it and discovers two pirates aboard. One is dead; the other, Israel Hands, is injured. Hands asks Jim to help sail the ship, but he secretly plans to attack him. Jim understands the risk but needs to get the vessel away from the mutineers. He must rely on his own judgment now, while the others remain at the stockade.

 The island changes the scale of Jim’s choices. On the ship he could follow adults, but on shore he becomes separated and must decide where to go. Ben Gunn is an unexpected meeting: he has survived alone, yet he is also desperate to return to other people. The stockade gives the loyal group a place to defend, but it cannot remove the danger outside its walls. Silver’s offer sounds practical because he promises safety in exchange for the map, but the captain knows that giving it away would not make the pirates trustworthy. Jim’s later decision to leave the stockade is risky and secretive. He hopes that moving the ship will help everyone, but he cannot know how dangerous Hands will be.

B2.text:
Once the Hispaniola anchors near the island, Jim goes ashore with the crew. He soon separates from the others. In the forest, he sees Long John Silver speak with Tom, an honest sailor. Tom refuses to join the pirates. Silver kills him, and Jim flees in fear. The boy then meets Ben Gunn, who has lived alone on the island since Flint’s crew left him behind. Ben hints that he has found the treasure and asks Jim to arrange a way home.

Jim returns to the loyal group at the stockade. The captain, doctor, squire, and their small party are preparing for an attack. Silver arrives to negotiate. He offers to spare them if they give him the map and surrender the ship. The captain refuses, so Silver’s men attack. The defenders hold the stockade, though they suffer losses. The doctor later goes out to treat wounded people, even though the pirates are still nearby.

Jim leaves the stockade alone and discovers Ben’s coracle, a tiny boat. He paddles to the Hispaniola, which is drifting loose. Two pirates remain aboard. One is dead, and Israel Hands is wounded. Hands pretends to cooperate so Jim will help him steer the ship. Jim knows he cannot fully trust him, but the ship must be moved out of the pirates’ reach. He takes the wheel and watches Hands closely. His decision to act alone gives him a chance to help his friends, but it also places him in immediate danger.

 The island changes the scale of Jim’s choices. On the ship he could follow adults, but on shore he becomes separated and must decide where to go. Ben Gunn is an unexpected meeting: he has survived alone, yet he is also desperate to return to other people. The stockade gives the loyal group a place to defend, but it cannot remove the danger outside its walls. Silver’s offer sounds practical because he promises safety in exchange for the map, but the captain knows that giving it away would not make the pirates trustworthy. Jim’s later decision to leave the stockade is risky and secretive. He hopes that moving the ship will help everyone, but he cannot know how dangerous Hands will be.

author: LessonCaptain (original retelling)
summary:
Jim and Israel Hands struggle for control of the Hispaniola. Jim climbs the mast to avoid Hands, but the injured sailor follows with a knife. Jim fires his pistol to protect himself, and Hands falls into the sea. Jim brings the ship to a quiet inlet and goes ashore. He is captured by Silver’s men, who are angry that he has taken the vessel. Silver stops them from harming Jim and keeps him close.

The next day the pirates go to find Flint’s treasure, forcing Jim to guide them with the map. Their confidence disappears when the marked place is empty. Ben Gunn has already moved the treasure. The pirates begin to turn against Silver. The doctor, squire, and their friends arrive, and the honest group regains control. Ben shows them where he hid the gold. They carry it to the ship and prepare to leave the island.

Silver stays with the party for the journey. At a port in Spanish America, he escapes with a small share of the treasure. Jim is relieved to be free of him but remembers that Silver sometimes protected him and sometimes threatened him. The crew returns to England. Jim’s part of the treasure gives him security, but the adventure has left him uneasy. Even after he is home, he dreams about the island, the sea, and the sound of the parrot calling for money.

 The final search changes the pirates’ mood from confidence to fear. The map seems to promise an easy reward, yet it cannot protect them from false expectations or from one another. Ben Gunn’s quiet work has already changed the outcome before Jim arrives at the empty place. Silver adapts when his authority weakens, while Jim must remember that protection and danger can come from the same person. The return voyage does not erase what happened. Jim has gained money, but he has also learned how violence and greed affect people long after a fight ends. His uneasy memories give the ending a serious tone. The adventure is complete, yet its emotional consequences remain with him.

B2.text:
Jim faces Israel Hands aboard the Hispaniola. Hands has pretended to help, but he plans to kill Jim and regain control of the ship. Jim climbs the rigging to stay out of reach. When Hands follows with a knife, Jim shoots him in self-defense. He then steers the ship into a sheltered place and leaves it where the pirates cannot easily use it.

Silver’s men capture Jim when he returns to land. Some want to punish him, but Silver protects him because Jim may still be useful. Silver takes charge of the treasure hunt and makes Jim accompany the pirates to the place shown on the map. On the way they find a skeleton arranged to point toward the treasure. The men grow frightened. At the marked spot, they discover an empty hole. Ben Gunn has already taken the treasure and hidden it elsewhere.

The failed search destroys Silver’s authority. His crew begins to rebel, but the doctor and the loyal sailors arrive in time to help Jim. They bring the treasure to the ship. Silver joins them rather than remain with the mutineers. On the return voyage he escapes at a port, taking some money with him. Jim is free, but he cannot simplify Silver into either a friend or an enemy: Silver had harmed people, manipulated the crew, and also saved Jim from immediate violence. Jim returns home with his share of the treasure. The island’s events continue to trouble his sleep, and the parrot’s cry remains part of his memories.

The adventure is complete, yet its emotional consequences remain with him.
